title: The Manuscript Sewn into a Coat
author: Viktor Frankl
wiifm: We end the week on the deepest layer of the operating system: the reason the whole machine keeps running at all. Viktor Frankl was a Viennese psychiatrist who spent years helping suicidal patients find a reason to live, and was then forced to test his own ideas in Nazi camps. As a mental health nursing student, Joe, you will meet his thinking on wards for the rest of your career. You will follow him from a precocious boyhood to Theresienstadt, Auschwitz and Dachau, and back to Vienna, and you will leave with his three sources of meaning, and an honest view of his limits.

ch.h: A boy who wrote to Freud
b: Viktor Frankl was born in Vienna on the twenty-sixth of March 1905, the middle of three children in a Jewish family. His father Gabriel was a civil servant in the ministry of social affairs, a strict, principled man. His mother Elsa was warm and pious. Vienna was the capital of an empire and the capital of a new science, psychoanalysis, and the boy was drawn to it early.

As a teenager he began writing to Sigmund Freud, then the most famous psychologist alive, and Freud wrote back. Frankl sent him a short paper, and in 1924 Freud had it published in the International Journal of Psychoanalysis. Frankl was nineteen.

Yet he was already drifting from Freud. The story he told later was that, at the age of about four, he had woken one night with the shock that he too would one day die. What troubled him was not fear of death but the question of whether death made life meaningless. Freud's picture of humans as driven by pleasure, and the rival school of Alfred Adler, which stressed the will to power, both seemed to him to leave something out: the will to meaning.

He was a clever, argumentative schoolboy who gave lectures to his classmates on philosophy and once, according to his own recollection, challenged a science teacher who described life as nothing but a process of combustion and oxidation. If that is all it is, the young Frankl asked, what is the meaning of life? The question would follow him for the rest of his career.
ch.cap: Teenage Frankl writes to Freud by lamplight in Vienna

b: Frankl studied medicine at the University of Vienna and joined Adler's circle, but his independence got him expelled from it in 1927. He turned instead to practical work. With colleagues, he set up free counselling centres for young people in Vienna and other cities. Teenage suicides tended to rise when school reports were handed out at the end of the year. In 1930, after a special campaign of counselling at report time, Vienna recorded no student suicides at all, a result that brought him attention across Europe.

After qualifying as a doctor in 1930 he trained in neurology and psychiatry. From 1933 to 1937 he ran the pavilion for suicidal women at the Steinhof psychiatric hospital in Vienna, and over those years he treated thousands of women who had tried, or were planning, to end their lives.

With each one he asked, in effect, the same question. What is keeping you alive? Often there was something: a child, a task left unfinished, a person they loved, a talent unused. He began to see that despair was frequently a loss of meaning rather than an excess of pain, and that helping someone find a reason to go on could steady them when nothing else did. He called his approach logotherapy, from the Greek logos, which he translated as meaning.
ch.cap: A pupil brings her school report to Frankl's counselling

b: In March 1938 Germany annexed Austria. Jewish doctors were barred from treating non-Jewish patients, and from 1940 Frankl became head of neurology at the Rothschild Hospital, the only hospital in Vienna still open to Jews. There, he later said, he falsified diagnoses to protect psychiatric patients from the Nazi euthanasia programme, labelling schizophrenia as aphasia so that they would not be killed.

In 1941 he was granted a visa to emigrate to the United States. It would have saved him, but it did not cover his elderly parents. He agonised over it. The story he told in his later memoir is that he came home one day to find on the table a piece of marble his father had picked up from the ruins of the main Vienna synagogue, destroyed in the pogrom of November 1938. It bore a fragment of the Ten Commandments: honour your father and your mother. He let the visa lapse.

He married Tilly Grosser, a nurse at the hospital, in December 1941. She soon became pregnant and, under Nazi rules, the couple were forced to end the pregnancy. In September 1942 Frankl, Tilly and his parents were deported to the Theresienstadt ghetto in Czechoslovakia.
ch.cap: The synagogue marble lies beside his unused visa

b: Theresienstadt was presented by the Nazis as a model settlement for elderly and prominent Jews. In reality it was a crowded transit camp of hunger and disease, from which tens of thousands were sent on to death camps. Frankl was put to work as a doctor. Drawing on his Steinhof experience, he organised a unit to help newcomers cope with the shock of arrival and to prevent suicides, working with the social worker Regina Jonas, the first woman ever ordained as a rabbi.

His father Gabriel died there in February 1943, of starvation and pneumonia. Frankl, who had kept a phial of morphine, gave it to his father to ease his breathing in his last hours. He later said that he felt, at that moment, that he had done everything he could, and that the decision to stay in Vienna had been right.
In October 1944 he and Tilly were put on a transport east. His mother followed shortly afterwards and was killed in the gas chambers at Auschwitz. He would not learn any of this for months.
ch.cap: In Theresienstadt, Frankl eases his dying father's breathing

b: The train reached Auschwitz on the nineteenth of October 1944. Frankl was separated from Tilly at the station. In his coat he had sewn the manuscript of his first book, setting out the ideas of logotherapy. He tried to persuade an older prisoner to let him keep it. The man shouted an obscenity, and the manuscript was taken with his clothes. Everything he had made of his life seemed to have been erased.

He was at Auschwitz only a few days before being sent on to Kaufering, a subcamp of Dachau in Bavaria, where prisoners were worked to death building underground bunkers for the German war effort. This matters, because he describes Auschwitz vividly in the book, but most of his experience was at Kaufering and later at Türkheim, another Dachau subcamp.

In the book he divides the prisoner's psychology into three phases. The first was shock on arrival, often mixed with a strange delusion of reprieve, the belief that somehow they would be spared. The second was the long middle phase of apathy: an emotional numbness that protected the mind but could also drain the will to live. The third, which he only reached later, was the disorientation of liberation.

He described a moment from his first hours that captures the shock. A fellow prisoner who had been there some time explained to the new arrivals what the chimney in the distance was for, and where those sent to the other line at the station had gone. Frankl wrote that he struck out his whole former life. And yet, he observed, people adapted to things they would have sworn they could never endure. They slept on bare boards packed nine to a bunk. They went without washing for months. Dostoevsky, he recalled, had defined man as a being who can get used to anything.
ch.cap: At Auschwitz, his sewn-in manuscript is torn away

ch.h: Talking to Tilly in the dark
b: The heart of the book is a scene on a march. Before dawn, prisoners stumbled through the snow and darkness to a worksite, guards shouting and driving them with rifle butts. The man beside Frankl muttered that he hoped their wives were in better camps and did not know what was happening to them. Frankl began to think of Tilly.

He saw her face, her smile, her encouraging look, more real to him than the dawn coming up. He realised, he wrote, that love is the ultimate and the highest goal to which a man can aspire, and that it reaches beyond the physical presence of the person loved. He did not know whether she was alive. It did not seem to matter to the comfort he took in her.

He saw the same pattern again and again. Prisoners who had a reason to live, a child waiting for them, work to finish, someone to see again, tended to hold on longer. Those who lost that reason often collapsed. He quoted Nietzsche: he who has a why to live for can bear almost any how. He also reported that in the week between Christmas 1944 and New Year 1945, deaths in the camp rose sharply, and the senior camp doctor attributed it to prisoners who had hoped to be home by Christmas losing heart when they were not.

For himself, his why was the lost manuscript. When he fell ill with typhus at Türkheim, he kept himself awake through the fevered nights by reconstructing it in shorthand on scraps of paper he had found.
ch.cap: On the dawn march, Frankl sees Tilly's face

ch.h: The last of the human freedoms
b: Frankl was liberated at Türkheim on the twenty-seventh of April 1945. When he returned to Vienna he learned that his mother had been killed at Auschwitz, his brother Walter had died there too, and Tilly had died at Bergen-Belsen, probably shortly after that camp was liberated. Of his immediate family, only his sister Stella, who had emigrated to Australia, survived.

In 1946, in about nine days, he dictated the account that became Man's Search for Meaning. It was first published in German under a title meaning A Psychologist Experiences the Concentration Camp. He had wanted it to appear anonymously, under his prisoner number, and agreed to put his name on it only so that it would carry more weight.

Its central claim is about freedom. Everything can be taken from a person, he wrote, except one thing: the freedom to choose one's attitude in any given set of circumstances. He had seen prisoners walk through the huts comforting others and giving away their last piece of bread. They were few, he admitted, but they proved the point. Between what happens to us and how we respond, some space remains.

He was careful not to romanticise suffering. Avoidable suffering should be avoided or ended. Only unavoidable suffering, faced with dignity, can become an achievement. And he refused the idea of collective guilt, insisting that there were decent people and indecent people in every group, guards included.

Liberation was not the joy prisoners had imagined. Frankl described men walking out of the gates into the spring meadows and feeling nothing at all, as if they had forgotten how to be glad. Some turned bitter, others felt that after what they had suffered they were entitled to do harm. Coming home to find no one waiting, he wrote, was perhaps the hardest experience of all. He himself, in letters to friends in the months after his return, wrote of feeling utterly alone and empty, and the work of rewriting his book became the thing that carried him.
ch.cap: In the hut, a prisoner gives away his bread

b: The second part of the book sets out logotherapy. Frankl argued that the primary drive in human beings is not pleasure or power but meaning, and that much modern distress comes from what he called the existential vacuum, a sense of emptiness and boredom. He thought it showed up in depression, addiction and aggression.

Meaning, he said, cannot be invented or handed out. It has to be discovered, and it is specific to each person and each moment. Ultimately, he argued, we should stop asking what we expect from life and realise that life is asking something of us. We answer by taking responsibility.

He named three main ways to find it. The first is by creating a work or doing a deed. The second is by experiencing something or encountering someone, above all through love. The third is by the attitude we take towards suffering that cannot be avoided. He gave the example of an elderly doctor who came to him in deep grief two years after his wife's death. Frankl asked what would have happened if he had died first. She would have suffered terribly, the man said. Then, said Frankl, you have spared her that, at the price of grieving for her yourself. The man shook his hand and left.

He also developed practical techniques. One was paradoxical intention: asking a patient with a fear, such as of sweating or blushing in public, to try deliberately to sweat as much as possible. The humour of the attempt often broke the cycle of anxiety, an idea that resembles later exposure methods in cognitive behavioural therapy.

He also coined the term Sunday neurosis, the low mood that some people feel when the busy week stops and the emptiness shows through. And he warned that happiness cannot be pursued directly. It must ensue, as a side effect of dedication to a cause greater than oneself or to a person one loves.
ch.cap: The grieving doctor shakes Frankl's hand and leaves

b: Frankl remarried in 1947, to Eleonore Schwindt, a young nurse, and they had a daughter, Gabriele. He led the neurology department of the Vienna Polyclinic for twenty-five years, lectured worldwide and took up mountaineering and, at sixty-seven, a pilot's licence. The English translation appeared in 1959 and was retitled Man's Search for Meaning in 1962. It has sold well over ten million copies. He died in Vienna on the second of September 1997, aged ninety-two.

The book deserves an honest note. The historian Timothy Pytell and others have pointed out that Frankl spent only a few days at Auschwitz, though readers often assume far longer, and that his account was shaped years after the events with a clear philosophical purpose. Survivors and scholars such as Lawrence Langer have warned that its message, that meaning helps people survive, can unfairly imply that those who died lacked it. Most died because of starvation, disease, selection and chance, whatever their inner life. Frankl himself wrote that the best of them did not return.

Pytell has also raised questions about experimental brain surgery Frankl carried out on Jewish patients who had attempted suicide at the Rothschild Hospital before deportation, which Frankl rarely discussed. Logotherapy itself has a modest evidence base compared with mainstream therapies, although meaning in life is now a well-studied predictor of wellbeing.

None of this erases what the book does. It offers a frightened or grieving person a question rather than a lecture: what is life asking of you now? Asked with care, at the right moment, on a ward or at a kitchen table, that question can still hold someone steady.
ch.cap: In old age, Frankl climbs the Alps at sunrise

take: People can bear almost any how if they have a reason. When motivation drops in yourself or a team, reconnect the task to a purpose people actually care about.
Frankl asked suicidal patients what held them to life. In care or in business, asking what matters most to a person often opens more than advice does.
You cannot always choose what happens, but you can choose your response. Pause before reacting to bad news, a hostile email or a setback.
Meaning comes from work and deeds, from love and encounters, and from facing unavoidable hardship with dignity. Check that your life draws on more than one.
Only unavoidable suffering can become meaningful. If pain or stress can be removed, remove it rather than enduring it.
Hope pinned to a specific date, like home by Christmas, can crush people when it passes. Set hope on direction and purpose rather than a date you cannot control.
Deliberately exaggerating a feared reaction can drain its power. A little humour about the fear often loosens its grip.
Meaning helps, but it did not decide who lived or died in the camps. Never imply that people who suffered or failed simply lacked the right attitude.
recall: It is Frankl's school of psychotherapy, named from the Greek logos, meaning meaning. It holds that the primary human drive is the will to meaning, and helps people discover meaning through work, love and the attitude they take to unavoidable suffering.
What did Frankl learn from his youth counselling and Steinhof work?

Targeted counselling around school-report time cut student suicides in Vienna to none in 1930. Treating thousands of suicidal women at Steinhof convinced him that despair often came from a loss of meaning, and that helping people find a reason to live could steady them.
Why did Frankl let his American visa lapse?

It did not cover his elderly parents and he did not want to abandon them. He later said a fragment of marble from a destroyed synagogue, bearing the commandment to honour your father and mother, settled his decision.
What are the three psychological phases Frankl described in the camps?
Shock on admission, often with a delusion of reprieve. Apathy and emotional numbness during camp life. And disorientation, bitterness or disillusionment after liberation.
What are the main criticisms of the book?

Historians such as Timothy Pytell note Frankl spent only days at Auschwitz and shaped his account later for a philosophical purpose. Others warn it can imply that those who died lacked meaning, when chance and brutality mostly decided survival.
note: Frankl's life is documented in his memoir Recollections, Haddon Klingberg's biography and the Viktor Frankl Institute. The marble fragment and the lost manuscript are Frankl's own accounts and cannot be independently verified. Timothy Pytell's critical biography challenges aspects of his self-presentation and raises his wartime brain surgery; Lawrence Langer has criticised the book's implications about survival. Logotherapy has limited trial evidence.

stories: In 1941 Viktor Frankl, a Jewish psychiatrist in Nazi Vienna, was granted a visa to the United States. It would have saved his life, but it did not cover his elderly parents. He agonised. The story he told later is that he came home one day to find on the table a piece of marble his father had picked up from the ruins of the main synagogue, destroyed in 1938. Carved on it was a fragment of the Ten Commandments: honour your father and your mother. He let the visa lapse. The next year the family was deported. It is Frankl's own account and cannot be independently checked.
The manuscript sewn into his coat

When Frankl arrived at Auschwitz in October 1944, he had sewn into his coat the manuscript of his first book, his life's work on meaning. He begged an older prisoner to let him keep it. The man shouted an obscenity, and the manuscript went with his clothes. Everything he had built seemed erased. Months later, at Türkheim, he caught typhus. Through the fevered nights he kept himself awake, and alive, by reconstructing the book in shorthand on scraps of paper. The lost book became his why. After liberation he dictated Man's Search for Meaning in about nine days.

An elderly doctor came to Frankl two years after his wife's death, still crushed by grief. Frankl did not offer comfort or a diagnosis. He asked a question. What would have happened if you had died first and she had survived you? Oh, she would have suffered terribly, the man said. Then, said Frankl, you have spared her that suffering, and the price is that you now grieve for her yourself. The man said nothing, shook Frankl's hand and left. His pain had not changed. Its meaning had. Frankl told it to show that even unavoidable suffering can carry a purpose.
biz: Ask what the client is protecting

Frankl found that despair was often a loss of meaning, and that asking what kept someone going steadied them. Debt Support Direct advisers are not therapists, but early in a call they can ask what matters most to the client: keeping the home, protecting the children, sleeping again. Build the plan around that answer and record it. Where a client mentions crisis or suicidal thoughts, follow a written escalation route, including Samaritans on 116 123 and the Mental Health Crisis Breathing Space scheme. This week, check every adviser knows that route and that the Debt and Mental Health Evidence Form process is documented.

Frankl's 1930 campaign worked because he noticed teenage suicides peaked when school reports came out, and put help there. Debt distress also has seasons: January after Christmas spending, the weeks after a bailiff or court letter, council tax reminders. Look at twelve months of Debt Support Direct enquiries and call notes to find your peaks, then staff up and add a short wellbeing check to scripts in those weeks. Measure call answer rates and vulnerability flags in peak weeks against quiet ones, so help is there when people need it most.
connects: Frankl built his survival philosophy on Nietzsche's line that he who has a why to live for can bear almost any how.
Frankl's last of the human freedoms, choosing one's attitude, restates Epictetus's teaching that we are disturbed not by events but by our judgements of them.
recap:
Viktor Frankl was born in Vienna in nineteen oh five. As a teenager he wrote letters to Sigmund Freud, who published one of his papers when he was nineteen. But Frankl was already asking a different question from Freud. Not what drives us towards pleasure, but what makes life meaningful.

As a young doctor he set up free counselling for students, and when he noticed that teenage suicides rose when school reports came out, he put help there. In nineteen thirty Vienna recorded no student suicides at all. Then he treated thousands of suicidal women, asking each one what was keeping her alive. A child, a task, a person. The first big idea grew from that work. Despair is often a loss of meaning, not just an excess of pain, and finding a reason can hold someone steady. He called it logotherapy.

When the Nazis took Austria, Frankl ran the only hospital still open to Jews. In nineteen forty one he was offered a visa to America that did not cover his parents. By his own account, a marble fragment from a ruined synagogue, carved with honour your father and your mother, decided it. He stayed. The family was deported. His father died in the ghetto, his mother and brother were killed at Auschwitz, and his young wife Tilly died at Bergen Belsen.

He arrived at Auschwitz with his book sewn into his coat. It was taken. He spent most of his imprisonment in subcamps of Dachau. On a freezing dawn march he thought of Tilly's face, not knowing if she was alive, and understood that love reaches beyond presence. The second idea came from what he saw around him. Prisoners with a reason to live, someone to see again, work to finish, tended to hold on longer. He quoted Nietzsche: he who has a why can bear almost any how.

The third idea is his most famous. Everything can be taken from a person except one thing, the freedom to choose one's attitude. He saw men give away their last bread. Between what happens and how we respond, some space remains.

The fourth idea is that meaning is found in three ways: through work, through love, and through the stance we take towards suffering we cannot avoid. Happiness cannot be chased. It ensues.

Historians note he was at Auschwitz only days, and that most who died had meaning too and simply had no chance. Frankl said the best did not return.

He died in nineteen ninety seven. His book still asks one gentle question.

The line to remember: stop asking what you expect from life, and ask what life is asking of you.
